title: An estimated risk score used as a regressor
question: When a risk score estimated in a prognostic cohort is used as a regressor for treatment-effect heterogeneity, does treating it as data understate the interval, and is the understatement worst at the tails of risk?
design: Logistic prognostic score from cohorts of 300 to 5000, used in a six-trial individual-data meta-regression with calibration drift; plug-in and bootstrap-propagated intervals for the treatment effect at the 10th, 50th and 90th risk percentiles. 6 cells, 500 replicates each.
answer: Little, given a prognostic cohort of about a thousand patients or more: propagating the score's estimation uncertainty widened intervals by at most 2.4%, and plug-in coverage stayed near nominal. With 300 cohort patients the widening reached 7% at the risk tails against about 1% at the median, confirming that the understatement is worst where recommendations are made, and plug-in coverage fell to 0.924. The registered rule (plug-in coverage at least 0.93 everywhere) was missed in that one scenario, so the refuting sentence fails as registered.
findings: Widening ratio 1.001 to 1.024 with cohorts of 1000 or 5000; 1.011 to 1.073 with 300.
Tails against median with 300: widening 1.065 to 1.073 against 1.011 to 1.012.
not_answered: Pairwise six-trial analysis; frequentist bootstrap rather than a joint or cut Bayesian model; well-specified score. Peer review has not been done.
estimand: Treatment log odds ratio at the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles of true risk
methods_compared: plug-in interval treating the score as data
interval adding bootstrap variance of the score
n_sim: 500 per scenario, 3,000 in total, each with 20 bootstrap refits
